name: So
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 5 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Carlin, Eithne. 1993. The So Language. Afrikanistische Monographien 2. Köln: Institut für Afrikanistik, Universität zu Köln. §2.3 'Stress', pp. 16-17 (also §1.1, p. 1). Rosetta Project (Long Now Foundation) excerpt scan on the Internet Archive, items (phonology, pp. 9-10, 15-23) and (ch. 1, pp. 1-8).
catalog_quote: So has variously been described as a stress-accent language and a tone language, or one where both play a role together. I found no evidence for So being a tone language. Tone has no distinctive role, neither on the lexical nor on the syntactic level. It seems to me, however, that stress-accent is important in So, not on the paradigmatic level, but rather on the syntagmatic level. Thus a lexical unit is not specified for accent in the lexicon as it is for other paradigmatic prosodic contrasts, that is, for example, length. Following Beckman (1986), stress-accent is an organizational feature in So and not a distinctive one. Within the domain of a bisyllabic word stem, stress falls on the first syllable, for example: 'lakʷan "child" If a derivative suffix is added, however, then stress generally falls on the final syllable, for example: lakʷa'n-a child-1.SG.POSS "my child" ko-ken-'k-as FUT-kill-IMPS-1.SG.OBJ "I will be killed." ʊrʊ'm-ac gather-VEN "gather up" It is surely no coincidence that the intonation contour rises clause-finally and that most accented syllables are found in an immediate pre-pausal position ... Compare the following examples: 'gʷes gʷa's-at ɛdɛ 'gʷas-t-uk women woman-SG certain woman-SG-GOA "women; a woman; a certain woman" 'nyet nye't-at ɛdɛ nye't-at-uk men man-SG certain man-SG-GOA "men; a man; a certain man"

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: The quotation was checked again. the reported passage is verbatim at lines 4758-4761 (Schrock 2014 §3.2 Tone, p. 100; page marker '100' at line 4749): 'And from within the Kuliak group, Carlin "found no evidence of So being a tone language" but rather that "stress-accent is important in So, not on the paradigmatic level, but rather on the syntagmatic level" (1993:16). Tone data on Nyang'ía is not yet available.' The excerpt file matches it. Status correction: the primary source is open. Glottolog's bib record 158245 for Carlin 1993 carries iaid=rosettaproject_teu_phon-1; the Long Now Foundation's Rosetta Project put excerpt scans of Carlin 1993 (600 ppi, ABBYY text) on the Internet Archive.…
new_statements.rule_in_words: According to Carlin (via Schrock), So is not a tone language; it has stress-accent, but stress is not lexically (paradigmatically) contrastive and operates at the syntagmatic (utterance/phrase) level. No source opened states which syllable of the word carries stress. A tertiary paraphrase of Heine 1976 (Wikipedia) adds that Proto-Kuliak primary stress could fall on any syllable and is retained in all Kuliak languages, while the secondary stress on the 2nd syllable shifted to the first syllable in Tepes; this is unverified and partly at odds with Carlin's characterization.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Only the unverified Wikipedia paraphrase of Heine 1976: Proto-Kuliak secondary stress on the 2nd syllable 'shifts to the first syllable in Tepes'. Nothing in an opened primary source.
new_statements.domain_note: Carlin's statement is about the syntagmatic (phrase/utterance) level versus the paradigmatic (lexical) level; no word-level placement rule is given. The quotation is second-hand (Schrock 2014 on Ik) and the Carlin monograph could not be opened.
new_statements.identity_note: Carlin 1993 and Heine 1975/1976 describe So chiefly from the Tepes (Tepeth, Mt Moroto) dialect, with Kadam (Mt Kadam) data in Heine's manuscript; Glottolog treats all under sooo1256 (Soo). Ethnologue/older sources also call the people Sor/Sorat. Nyang'i (nyan1313) is a separate Kuliak language, not a variety of So.

sources.citation: Wikipedia, 'Kuliak languages' (raw wikitext, downloaded 2026-09-17), paragraph paraphrasing Heine 1976 The Kuliak languages of Eastern Uganda
sources.note: Tertiary paraphrase: 'Heine reconstructs two classes of stress in Proto-Kuliak: primary, which could occur in any position and remains in place in all Kuliak languages, and secondary, which always occurred on the 2nd syllable of a word, and remains there in Ik and Nyang'i, but shifts to the first syllable in Tepes.' No page cited; not verified against Heine 1976.
